beginner.title: In a nutshell
beginner.scale.minorPentatonic: 5 notes that almost always sound right over minor, rock or blues songs. The scale to start improvising with.
beginner.scale.majorPentatonic: 5 bright, safe notes over major songs: folk, country, pop.
beginner.scale.blues: The minor pentatonic plus a “blue” note (♭5) that adds tension. Slide through it; don't stop on it.
beginner.scale.naturalMinor: All 7 notes of the minor key. More colour than the pentatonic, but more notes to place carefully.
beginner.scale.major: All 7 notes of the major key (do-re-mi…). Every chord of the key is built from them.
beginner.scale.mixolydian: The major scale with a lowered 7th (♭7). It fits rock, blues and country songs that use a ♭VII chord or 7th chords.
beginner.roots: Orange squares are the root, the “home” note. Ending a phrase on it feels resolved.
beginner.position: A position fits under your hand without moving (about 4 frets). Learn one, then move to the next with ▶: they link along the neck.
beginner.wholeNeck: Every note of the scale on the neck. Pick a position with ▶ to focus on one area.
beginner.fullScale: 7-note scale: shown across the whole neck. Find the roots first, then the notes around them.
beginner.intervals: In “intervals” mode, each note shows its distance from the root: 1 = root, ♭3 = minor third (sad colour), 3 = major third (happy colour), 5 = fifth (solid), ♭7 = seventh (bluesy).
beginner.keyContext: Working key: {key}. The scale starts on {tonic}.
accompany.original: Original rhythms and sounds, generated on the phone: no copyrighted recordings.
styleExplain.blues: Blues: shuffle feel (swung eighths), 7th chords, walking bass. Improvise with the minor pentatonic or blues scale of the key.
styleExplain.rock: Rock: straight eighths, power chords, snare on 2 and 4. The minor pentatonic almost always works.
styleExplain.folk: Folk: gentle strumming, open chords, little tension. Major pentatonic or major scale.
styleExplain.country: Country: “boom-chick”, alternating root–fifth bass. Major pentatonic, with touches of blues.
prog.folkI_V_vi_IV: Folk / pop I – V – vi – IV
prog.countryI_IV_V: Country I – IV – V (2 bars each)
understand.circleHelp: Tap a key to choose it. Highlighted cells are the 6 chords “in the family”: the key, its neighbours (a fifth either side) and their relative minors.
fn.explain: ⌂ tonic = rest, “home”. ↗ subdominant = moving away. ⚡ dominant = tension that wants to return home.
understand.majorExplain: Major or minor? A major key sounds bright; its relative minor (3 semitones lower) uses exactly the same notes but rests on another “home”, hence a darker colour.
understand.minorExplain: Major or minor? A minor key sounds darker; its relative major (3 semitones higher) has the same notes. In minor, the 7th is often raised to get a major V (e.g. E major in A minor) that pulls harder back home.
understand.analysisHelp: Type chords (Am F C G, or Lam Fa Do Sol): the app suggests the key, each chord's role and scales to improvise with.
analysis.relativeExplain: These two keys are relatives: they share exactly the same notes. What decides is the chord the song “rests” on (often the first and last). Good news: the same pentatonic works for both.
scaleReason.pentatonicSafe: the safest choice: 5 notes, no “trap” note
scaleReason.fullScale: every note of the chords, for richer melodies
scaleReason.relativeSame: same notes, seen from the relative key
settings.inputHelp: USB interface, external mic or line input: choose it here (names appear after allowing the microphone).
settings.adaptiveHelp: The app learns the room's background noise and ignores what's below it. Sensitivity stays the minimum.
key.ambiguous: Key: {a} or {b} (same notes, to be confirmed)
play.speakerNotice: Backing on the speaker: the mic hears it too. Detection continues, but a chord identical to the loop's is flagged and kept out of the history. For reliable detection, use headphones or an audio interface.
play.echo: ≈ probably the backing track (same chord as the loop)
tuner.title: Tuner
tuner.unstable: Unstable signal… let a single string ring
tuner.help: One string at a time, let it ring. The needle turns green between −5 and +5 cents. Chords and noise are ignored.
calib.title: Guided calibration
calib.micNeeded: Allow the microphone to calibrate, then try again.
calib.silenceText: Don't play for 3 seconds: we're measuring the room's background noise.
calib.chordText: Strum a chord (e.g. A minor) as you normally would and let it ring for 4 seconds.
calib.advice.tooQuiet: Sound is too quiet: move the phone closer or raise the interface gain.
calib.advice.clipping: Sound is clipping: lower the interface gain or move the phone away.
calib.advice.noisyRoom: The room is noisy: the STABLE profile will avoid mistakes.
calib.advice.unclearChord: The chord isn't clear: check your tuning (Tuner tab) and let all strings ring.
calib.advice.tryInterface: For better results: a USB audio interface or a mic closer to the guitar.
calib.advice.allGood: All good: recognition can be responsive.
calib.applied: {profile} profile and sensitivity applied. You can change them in Settings.
profileHelp.fast: Shows the chord in about 0.25 s (measured on test signals). Best with an audio interface in a quiet room; also follows fast changes, so it may change its mind more often.
profileHelp.balanced: About 0.5 s (measured on test signals). A good compromise for most situations.
profileHelp.stable: About 0.75 s (measured on test signals). Holds steady in noise and ignores brief hesitations: for a phone mic in a lively room.
settings.channelHelp: 2-input interface (e.g. PreSonus): pick the input your guitar is plugged into.
settings.channelsSeen: Channels provided by the current input: {n}. If it's 1, the browser receives a mono signal.
settings.echoHelp: May reduce the backing heard by the mic when it plays from the phone speaker, without removing it completely. Useless with headphones; may degrade the guitar sound.
accompany.speakerWarning: Speaker: the mic also hears the loop. Chord detection stays on but cautious; to play and be recognised at the same time, use headphones or an audio interface.
output.speaker: Phone speaker
outputHelp.headphones: The loop goes to your headphones: the mic only hears your guitar, detection stays fully active.
outputHelp.interface: Guitar into the interface, loop on its headphone output: reliable simultaneous detection.
outputHelp.speaker: The mic will hear the loop: chords identical to the loop's are flagged, not counted.
world.title: Chord world: tap a neighbouring island to go there
world.hint: Tap a neighbouring island: Pik jumps there (on the next beat if the metronome is running). Paths show how the chords are related; drag to explore.
edgeWhy.resolution: {from} → {to}: resolution. The chord relaxes a fifth lower, like coming home.
edgeWhy.dominant: {from} → {to}: dominant. {to} builds tension that pulls back to {from}.
edgeWhy.diatonic: {from} → {to}: both chords belong to the same key; the move sounds natural.
edgeWhy.relative: {from} → {to}: relative. Almost the same notes, a brighter or darker colour.
edgeWhy.commonTones: {from} → {to}: two shared notes make a very smooth move.
edgeWhy.borrowed: {from} → {to}: borrowed from the parallel mode (major ↔ minor). An unexpected colour, common in rock and pop.
edgeWhy.modulation: {from} → {to}: modulation. {to} is the dominant of a neighbouring key: we move to another harmonic “country”.
settings.worldHelp: The world changes the scenery, colours, particles, animation style and Pik's outfit. Jazz and Pop are visual worlds: their dedicated backing doesn't exist yet.
gallery.title: World gallery
gallery.help: The six worlds and Pik's outfits, to check how they look on your screen.
